props.title: Host
props.initialSlug: Innovative Zoom-based horror film shot during lockdown

sections.content: **Host (2020)** (2020) revolutionized pandemic-era filmmaking by turning Zoom's limitations into pure terror. Shot entirely through video calls during lockdown, it follows six friends who conduct an ill-fated online séance. The film brilliantly builds on found footage foundations laid by **The Blair Witch Project** (1999) and **Paranormal Activity** (2007), but innovates by restricting itself to desktop horror like Unfriended (2014). Director Rob Savage maximizes everyday tech features - screen freezes, connection drops, chat messages - to amplify tension. At 56 minutes, it's ruthlessly efficient.

sections.content: The COVID-19 pandemic forced filmmakers to get creative with remote production. While **Host** (2020) set the standard, others followed: **Language Lessons** (2021) crafted an intimate drama through video lessons, **Social Distance** (2020) anthology series captured isolation stories, and **Malcolm & Marie** (2021) proved you could film during lockdown with minimal crew. These constraints sparked innovation in "screen life" storytelling - films taking place entirely through devices.

Desktop horror emerged before the pandemic with films like **Open Windows** (2014) and **Unfriended: Dark Web** (2018). But **Host** (2020) perfected the form by grounding supernatural scares in relatable pandemic anxiety. Every glitch and lag spike triggers dread. When characters break social distancing rules, we feel genuine fear. The film taps into our increased dependence on video calls and digital connection. SUBHEAD: Evolution of Found Footage Horror

sections.content: **Host** (2020) represents the latest evolution in found footage horror. From **Cannibal Holocaust** (1980) to **[REC]** (2007) to **Paranormal Activity** (2007), the genre adapts to new technology. Webcams brought us **V/H/S** (2012), smartphones enabled **Cloverfield** (2008), and now video conferencing platforms create new opportunities for scares. Each technological shift forces directors to justify why characters keep filming - **Host** solves this by making the recording inherent to the medium.
